playbook: Read this first: every group below was found through public search results, not by joining. Facebook hides most group details behind a login, so before joining, open each group's About tab and record the member count, privacy, rules and the date of the newest post. Drop any group with no posts in the last 60 days.

Who joins: join as the Mitchell Homes business Page wherever the group allows Pages (admins can turn this on). Where it does not, join from a named team member's personal profile with "New Home Consultant at Mitchell Homes" in the work info. Even in groups that allow the Page, a named consultant usually gets better replies when answering questions in the comments.

Ask before posting: after joining, read the rules and pinned posts, then send an admin the short outreach note. Do not post anything that mentions Mitchell until an admin says yes or the rules clearly allow it. Log the answer the same day.

Residents only groups (Lake Gaston Community Information, some newcomer clubs): only a team member who lives there joins, or ask the admin for an exception in writing. Never misstate where anyone lives.
Give before asking: spend the first two weeks in each group only answering questions in the comments. Answer the question fully first; mention Mitchell last, if at all.
One helpful post per group per week at most. Most groups will be better served by one a month.
Never post the same text in many groups on the same day. Rotate the five posts, change the opening line for each group, and spread groups across different days.
Answer every comment within one business day. If someone asks about price, the fall offer or their own land, thank them and offer a call; do not quote numbers in the group.
Always disclose: "I work with Mitchell Homes." Never message members who did not ask.
Links: only where the rules allow them, one link at the end, using the UTM links in this file. Where links are not allowed, delete the link line and end at the comments line.

Fair housing: never describe a town, county or neighborhood as a good, safe, growing or desirable place to live, and never answer "where should we move" questions. Mitchell builds on land the buyer already owns and does not sell land, so never offer, suggest or rank lots or areas. Point people to their county planning and health departments instead.
No prices, savings figures, Design Dollars or other offers in groups. Those belong on a call with a New Home Consultant.
Photos: real Mitchell homes only. Real Mitchell homeowners are approved for organic posts.
Spam check: skip or leave groups that are mostly land flipper posts, "we buy land" ads, or a wall of business ads with no replies. The Horry County business group network below is flagged for this.

Track every group in one sheet: name, URL, admin, date joined, date asked, admin answer, Page allowed (yes or no), links allowed (yes or no), business post day, last post date, post used, comments, calls booked. Review monthly and drop groups that produce nothing after three posts.

posts.title: What a perc test tells you before you build
posts.fits: Land for sale groups, homesteading and rural groups, lake groups, local community groups that allow helpful posts.
posts.body:
Own land, or looking at a parcel, and wondering whether it will take a septic system? A soil evaluation, often called a perc test, answers that.

How it usually works:
1. An evaluator digs test holes where the septic field might go and reads the soil layers.
2. The results show whether a conventional system fits, whether an alternative system is needed, or whether that spot will not work.
3. The approved septic area, plus the setback distances your state sets, shapes where the house, the well and the driveway can go.

Your county health department is the place to start. In some areas a licensed private evaluator can do the work.

If you are buying land, try to get the evaluation done before closing. If you already own land, it is a good question to bring to any builder's first site visit.

I work with Mitchell Homes. We have built on land people already own since 1992, and I'm happy to answer questions in the comments.

Curious what a home on your land could look like? Our eight-question quiz paints one for you: https://mitchellhomesliving.com/portrait?utm_source=facebook_group&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=fall26_portrait&utm_content=fbg_perc

posts.title: No public water or sewer? How the well and septic fit together
posts.fits: Homesteading and rural groups, lake groups, land groups, county community groups.
posts.body:
No public water or sewer at the road? That is normal for rural land. Here is the order it usually goes when you build.

First, the soil evaluation shows where a septic system can go.
Next, the well site is planned at the required distance from the septic area. Your county or state health department sets those distances.
Then the house, the driveway and the power line are placed around both.

What changes the cost: how deep the well needs to go, which depends on the ground where you are, and which type of septic system your soil allows. Ask a well driller and a septic installer who work in your county what is typical there.

I work with Mitchell Homes, and we build on land people already own. Our Behind the Build episode on well and septic walks through all of this; it is on the Mitchell Homes YouTube channel. Questions welcome below.

If you'd like to see a home on your land, our eight-question quiz paints a Home Portrait for you: https://mitchellhomesliving.com/portrait?utm_source=facebook_group&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=fall26_portrait&utm_content=fbg_wellseptic

posts.title: Building on land you own: the site costs to ask about
posts.fits: Land groups, building a home groups, relocation groups, local community groups.
posts.body:
When you build on land you own, the house is one number and the land has its own line items. Ask any builder which of these are in their price and which are separate:

1. Soil evaluation and the septic system, or the sewer tap
2. Well, or the water tap
3. Clearing and grading for the house and driveway
4. The driveway itself
5. Running power from the road
6. Survey, permits and county fees

These vary a lot from one lot to the next, which is why a site visit matters before anyone gives you a firm number.

I work with Mitchell Homes. We build on land people already own, so these questions come up often. Ask anything in the comments.

Our eight-question quiz paints a Home Portrait of a home on your land: https://mitchellhomesliving.com/portrait?utm_source=facebook_group&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=fall26_portrait&utm_content=fbg_sitecosts

posts.title: Can the land you own count toward building on it?
posts.fits: Only groups whose rules allow business posts, or on the admin's business post day. It names the SimplyMitchell program. Virginia and Southern Maryland groups use the first link; Carolinas groups use the quiz link.
posts.body:
A question we hear a lot: can the land I already own count as my down payment?

With a traditional construction loan, it depends on the lender. Some count the equity in land you own toward the down payment. Ask how they value the land, whether it needs to be paid off first, and how many closings the loan involves.

At Mitchell Homes we do it differently. With SimplyMitchell, building on land you own means zero down, zero closing costs and no construction loan, because Mitchell self funds every build.

I work with Mitchell Homes and I'm happy to answer questions in the comments.

Virginia and Southern Maryland: https://simplymitchellhomes.com/math?utm_source=facebook_group&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=fall26_fourbuyers&utm_content=fbg_downpayment
North and South Carolina: https://mitchellhomesliving.com/portrait?utm_source=facebook_group&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=fall26_portrait&utm_content=fbg_downpayment

posts.title: Seven things to check before you buy a lot to build on
posts.fits: Land for sale and land buyer groups, relocation groups, homesteading groups, local community groups.
posts.body:
Looking at a lot to build on? Seven things to check before you commit:

1. Access. Legal road frontage or a recorded easement.
2. Septic. A soil evaluation, or public sewer at the road.
3. Water. A public tap, or room for a well.
4. Power. How far the nearest line is from where the house would sit.
5. Zoning and setbacks. What the county allows and how far back the house must sit.
6. Flood zone and wetlands. Check the county map.
7. Deed restrictions. Covenants or HOA rules recorded on the property.

Your county planning office, the health department and a survey settle most of these.

I work with Mitchell Homes. We don't sell land; we build on land people already own, so we see these questions often. Ask away in the comments.

No land yet? That is fine. Our eight-question quiz paints a Home Portrait either way: https://mitchellhomesliving.com/portrait?utm_source=facebook_group&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=fall26_portrait&utm_content=fbg_buildable
